html:
The Battle of Sekigahara was fought on 21 October 1600 at Sekigahara, a valley in today's Gifu Prefecture in central Japan. Tokugawa Ieyasu beat a coalition of rival lords led by Ishida Mitsunari and became master of Japan.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who had finished the unification begun by Oda Nobunaga, died in 1598. He left a five-year-old heir and a council of regents. Ieyasu, the richest of them, soon acted like the ruler. Mitsunari gathered the lords of the west to stop him in the heir's name. The two armies, each of roughly 80,000 men, met in fog where the main roads between east and west pass through the hills. But Ieyasu had been writing secretly to lords on the other side. At midday Kobayakawa Hideaki, on a hill above the western flank, changed sides and charged his own allies. The western army fell apart within hours. Mitsunari was caught and beheaded.

Ieyasu took land from his enemies and gave it to his supporters. In 1603 the emperor named him shogun. The Tokugawa shogunate ended the wars of the Sengoku age and ruled Japan in peace, mostly closed to the world, until 1868.
